topic: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
parentTitle: Physical Health, Transitions and End of Life
title: Constipation
blurb: Recognise constipation as a potentially fatal risk for people with a learning disability, monitor bowels accurately and escalate red flags early.
question: Ava, 29, has a profound learning disability and no speech. Over two days she has become restless, is pressing on her stomach and pushing food away. Her bowel chart shows no stool for six days. Staff think she is 'being difficult'. What is the most likely cause, and what should the nurse do?

teach.body: People with learning disabilities are more likely to have constipation than other people, and may not be able to say so. Untreated, it can lead to faecal impaction, overflow, vomiting, bowel obstruction, twisting of the bowel and septicaemia, and LeDeR reviews still find constipation contributing to deaths. In plain English: a bowel problem that most people treat at home can kill someone whose discomfort is missed or dismissed as behaviour.
teach.cite: PHE, Constipation: making reasonable adjustments (2016); LeDeR 2023

head: Cause
Example
rows: No privacy, rushed or changed routine
teach.caption: PHE: people with more severe learning disabilities are at even higher risk.

bands.label: Sausage with cracks: easy to pass
Smooth, soft sausage: easy to pass

teach.caption: Types 3-4 are easiest to pass. Watery stool after days without a proper stool may be overflow around impaction.

teach.body: 'Bowels opened' tells nobody anything. Record the date and time, the Bristol type, the amount, and any pain, straining, blood, soiling or change in behaviour. Know the person's usual pattern from family and the hospital passport. A good chart lets staff spot a trend early, and makes sure bowel history follows the person when they move between services, a failing highlighted in serious case reviews.
teach.cite: PHE constipation guidance; NICE CKS constipation

teach.caption: Constipation can also increase seizures in people with epilepsy, and vomiting raises aspiration risk.

teach.body: Ava cannot say she is in pain, so she shows it: restlessness, pressing her abdomen and refusing food. Six days without stool makes constipation the likely cause. The nurse treats this as a physical health problem, not behaviour: she assesses her abdomen and observations, checks her medicines for constipating effects, and arranges a same-day GP review. She also agrees a bowel plan: fluids, fibre, activity, a regular private toilet routine and prescribed laxatives, with the chart reviewed daily.

teach.text: Liquid stool after days of no proper bowel movement is often overflow around impacted faeces, not diarrhoea. Giving an antidiarrhoeal makes impaction worse. And clozapine: MHRA warns it can cause potentially fatal intestinal obstruction, faecal impaction and paralytic ileus; constipation in someone on clozapine must be recognised early and treated actively.

teach.caption: Extra fluid alone does not help unless the person is dehydrated. Laxatives are prescribed and reviewed, not added informally.

items: Fluids spread through the day; account for drooling, sweating and mouth breathing.
Gradually increase fibre that the person enjoys, with their involvement.
Daily movement: even repositioning and moving around helps the bowel.
A warm, private, unhurried toilet routine; footstool and good seating.
Medicine review for constipating drugs; prescribed laxatives reviewed regularly.
Constipation is common in people with LD and can kill through impaction, obstruction and aspiration.
Constipating medicines: antipsychotics (especially clozapine), antidepressants, anticonvulsants, opioids.
Record Bristol type, amount, date and concerns, not 'bowels opened'.
Behaviour change may be pain from constipation.
Liquid leakage after no proper stool may be overflow: do not give antidiarrhoeals.

summary: You can now explain why constipation is dangerous for people with a learning disability, record bowel habits with the Bristol Stool Chart and recognise behaviour change as possible pain. You can spot overflow and clozapine-related red flags and escalate them urgently.

A.q: Staff supporting Ryan, 24, have recorded 'bowels opened' each day for a week. What should a useful bowel chart record?
options: The name of the staff member who helped him each time
The time, Bristol stool type, amount and any concerns
Whether he used the toilet or a commode on each day
The number of glasses of water he drank each morning
A.why: A bowel chart should record date and time, Bristol type, amount and concerns (pain, straining, blood) so problems are spotted early.

whyNot.0: Staff names do not describe bowel health.
whyNot.2: Toilet or commode use does not show stool type or amount.
whyNot.3: Fluid intake matters but belongs on a fluid chart and is not a bowel record.

A.q: Which Bristol Stool Chart types suggest constipation?
options: Types 1 and 2
Types 3 and 4
Types 5 and 6
Types 6 and 7
A.why: Types 1 (separate hard lumps) and 2 (lumpy sausage) suggest constipation; types 3 and 4 are easiest to pass.

whyNot.1: Types 3 and 4 are the easiest to pass.
whyNot.3: Types 6 and 7 suggest diarrhoea, illness or overflow.

A.q: A nurse is reviewing the medicines of Nathan, 42, who has a learning disability and schizophrenia. Which medicine has an MHRA warning about potentially fatal intestinal obstruction?
options: Sertraline
Lamotrigine
Clozapine
Levothyroxine
A.why: MHRA (October 2017): clozapine can impair intestinal peristalsis, from very common constipation to rare, sometimes fatal, obstruction, faecal impaction and paralytic ileus.

whyNot.0: Sertraline is not the subject of this MHRA warning.
whyNot.1: Lamotrigine is not the subject of this warning.
whyNot.3: Levothyroxine treats hypothyroidism, itself a cause of constipation; it is not the drug warned about.

B.q: Ava, 29, has a profound learning disability and no speech. Over two days she has become restless, presses on her abdomen and refuses food. She has not opened her bowels for six days. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Constipation causing abdominal pain
A change in her usual behaviour pattern
Low mood after a change of staff
A dislike of her new menu choices
B.why: Behaviour change may be how Ava communicates pain. With no stool for six days and abdominal pressing, constipation is the most likely cause and needs assessment.

whyNot.1: Labelling it behaviour is diagnostic overshadowing; the cause must be found.
whyNot.2: Nothing suggests a mood disorder; the physical signs point to the bowel.
whyNot.3: Food refusal with abdominal pressing suggests pain, not taste.

B.q: Bethany, 46, has a learning disability and has not had a proper bowel movement for eight days. Staff now report frequent small amounts of liquid stool and ask for loperamide. What should the nurse do?
options: Give the loperamide and record each stool
Increase her fluids and stop her laxatives
Start a stool sample for gastroenteritis
Withhold it and seek review for impaction
B.why: Liquid leakage after days without a proper stool suggests overflow around impacted faeces. An antidiarrhoeal would worsen impaction; she needs medical assessment.

whyNot.0: Loperamide slows the bowel and worsens impaction.
whyNot.1: Stopping laxatives is wrong when impaction is likely.
whyNot.2: Infection is less likely given the eight days without stool.

B.q: Noah, 27, has a learning disability and constipation. A support worker says he refuses prune juice and high-fibre cereal. What is the best approach?
options: Agree acceptable food and drink with him and review
Add prune juice to his meals without telling him
Ask the GP to double his laxative dose straight away
Record that he refuses and stop offering fibre
B.why: Person-centred bowel care involves Noah in finding foods and drinks he will accept, using accessible information, and reviews treatment if diet is not enough.

whyNot.1: Covertly adding food overrides his choice without a lawful basis.
whyNot.2: Doubling the dose without review skips the person-centred plan.
whyNot.3: Giving up leaves his constipation unmanaged.

C.q: Oliver, 51, has a profound learning disability and takes clozapine. He has had no stool for four days, has vomited twice, and his abdomen is distended and tender. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Give a stimulant laxative and review in 24 hours
Arrange urgent medical assessment the same day
Withhold his next clozapine dose and observe him
Offer clear fluids and repeat the bowel chart tomorrow
C.why: Vomiting, distension and tenderness with constipation in a person on clozapine may be obstruction or ileus, which can be fatal. MHRA stresses early recognition and active treatment; he needs urgent assessment.

whyNot.0: Stimulant laxatives can be harmful in obstruction and waiting 24 hours is unsafe.
whyNot.2: Withholding without medical input does not address possible obstruction.
whyNot.3: Delay risks a fatal bowel complication.

C.q: Amelia, 34, has a learning disability, uses a wheelchair and takes several constipating medicines. She has had recurrent constipation. What is the best plan?
options: A regular enema each week to keep her bowels clear
A high-fluid diet with no other changes to her care
A bowel plan covering fluids, fibre, activity and review
An increase in laxatives whenever staff notice a problem
C.why: PHE recommends a holistic, person-centred bowel plan: fluids, fibre, movement, toileting routine and position, medicine review and prescribed laxatives where needed, with regular review.

whyNot.0: Routine enemas are invasive and do not address the causes.
whyNot.1: Extra fluid alone does not help unless dehydrated (NICE CKS).
whyNot.3: Ad hoc increases without a plan or review are unsafe.

C.q: Simon, 38, has a learning disability and epilepsy. His seizures have increased over a week with no change in medicines. Staff note he has strained without passing stool for five days and is off his food. What should the nurse consider first?
options: A new psychiatric illness affecting his sleep
An increase in his anti-seizure medicine dose
A side effect of his usual anti-seizure medicine
Constipation as a trigger for his extra seizures
C.why: PHE notes people with epilepsy may have more seizures when constipated. Five days of straining with appetite loss points to a treatable trigger.

whyNot.1: Raising the dose before treating a clear trigger adds side effects.
whyNot.2: His medicines are unchanged, so a new trigger is more likely.

reteach.title: When the gut speaks through behaviour
reteach.question: How might someone who cannot talk tell you they are constipated?

blocks.h: Look for the signs, not the words
blocks.body: Pressing or hitting the abdomen, restlessness, agitation or self-harm, refusing food, sleep problems, sitting oddly, more seizures, or vomiting. PHE notes research linking chronic constipation with behaviour problems, including self-harm. Check the bowel chart before calling anything 'behaviour'.

blocks.text: Never assume liquid stool means the bowel is empty: overflow is a sign of impaction.

explain.body: Impaction, overflow, obstruction, twisting of the bowel, septicaemia and aspiration from vomiting. Serious case reviews describe deaths from complications of faecal impaction in people with learning disabilities.

test.q: Which complication of constipation is most likely to cause death?
options: Haemorrhoids caused by repeated straining
Loss of appetite and weight
Bowel obstruction with septicaemia
Mild abdominal cramps after meals
test.why: Untreated constipation can progress to impaction, obstruction, bowel ischaemia and septicaemia, which can be fatal.

whyNot.0: Haemorrhoids cause pain and bleeding but are rarely fatal.
whyNot.1: Appetite loss matters but is not the main fatal risk.
whyNot.3: Cramps are a symptom, not a fatal complication.

explain.body: Antipsychotics, antidepressants and anticonvulsants (PHE), opioids and anticholinergics. Clozapine carries an MHRA warning about fatal obstruction.

test.q: Which group of medicines does PHE guidance list as having a negative effect on bowel movement?
options: Antipsychotics, antidepressants and anticonvulsants
Antibiotics, antifungals and antivirals
Statins, ACE inhibitors, beta blockers and calcium blockers
Insulin, metformin and gliclazide
test.why: PHE names antipsychotic, antidepressant and anticonvulsant medication as having a negative effect on bowel movement.

whyNot.2: These are not the groups PHE lists.
whyNot.3: Diabetes medicines are not the groups PHE names.

explain.body: Liquid stool leaking around hard impacted faeces after days without a proper stool. Antidiarrhoeals are harmful here; the impaction needs treating.

test.q: A woman who has not had a proper stool for a week now has small amounts of liquid stool. What is the most likely explanation?
options: A viral gastroenteritis
Overflow around impaction
A side effect of fibre
Normal recovery of the bowel
test.why: Liquid leakage after a week without a proper stool suggests overflow around impacted faeces.

whyNot.0: The preceding week without stool points to impaction.
whyNot.2: Fibre does not cause this pattern.
whyNot.3: This is a warning sign, not recovery.

explain.body: Holistic plan: fluids, fibre, activity, toileting routine and position, medicine review. Laxatives (NICE CKS): bulk-forming, then osmotic, then stimulant; in opioid-induced constipation avoid bulk-forming.

test.q: A man has constipation caused by morphine. Which laxative type should be avoided according to NICE CKS?
options: Osmotic, such as macrogol
Stimulant, such as senna
Osmotic, such as lactulose
Bulk-forming (ispaghula)
test.why: NICE CKS: in opioid-induced constipation use an osmotic or stimulant laxative; do not use bulk-forming laxatives.

whyNot.0: Osmotic laxatives are recommended for opioid-induced constipation.
whyNot.1: Stimulant laxatives are recommended for opioid-induced constipation.
whyNot.2: Lactulose is an osmotic laxative, an option for opioid-induced constipation.
